blocks.cap: The riverside memorial as the last lantern goes out

blocks.p: The last lantern on the river went out a few metres from the pier. It did not float away. It simply stopped being lit. Behind it, where the second light had leaned close to watch, something on the far side let out a breath. Rei felt it on his face.

His father used to say that the truth of any account comes down to a single line. Rei found that line now, standing on the gravel with his chest bent around the strain of the Axis. The light at the centre could not hold both brothers much longer. The seam could not stay this open until morning without tearing. And the chair was speaking.

It did not speak in the Healer's voice, or in Gin's. It spoke in Rei's own voice. That was the thing he had not understood from his notes, and understood now in his body. It used the voice he thought in. You could. You fit. Sit down and it stops hurting everyone. An empty office cannot be argued into being filled. A living register has to agree to carry it, and the only voice that can agree is the voice of the one who will sit. The Healer could not put him in the chair. The thing watching through Kaito's eyes could not. And Gin, with every sentence he stole back, could not keep him out.

So the whole month had come down to this. Every knot in the ledger. Every soft-voiced woman with a bowl of soup. The six-year lean of an empty office on a sleeping ward. All of it had brought him to this rail on this night, then stepped back and left him alone with his own voice.
He felt the pulls one after another, the way he had felt the registers test his walled-off places in Shin-Ōkubo.
First the warm downward pull of the chair. It felt exactly like being tired enough to lie down in snow.
Then the sick lurch of looking at his brother's hands and thinking, for half a second, he said let it be him. He hated how much lighter that half second felt.
Then the black temptation to walk away up the embankment and let the wall do what walls do when no one holds them.

And under all of it, something worse and quieter. The Axis was straining in his chest like a rope. He could pull. He could pull until it snapped and the chair came apart with it. Then there would be no chair for anyone, only a hole, and no one would ever be made to sit.

"You are counting," the Healer said gently. It was watching his face. "Good. Count. A seat taken is every other seat untaken. A city saved this way is a city not saved that way. A brother kept is a chair left empty. A chair filled is a brother spent. There is no reading of the ledger, however long you stare, in which the columns come out even."
Rei understood the trap completely. Understanding it did not get him out of it.

He thought about the face at the centre of the light. The tired young man in the old coat, who had answered one question and was now spending himself to keep two strangers off a chair. The seat I became. He thought about the ledger the Healer kept describing, with its neat columns. There was no column in it for that man. Every sum the Healer had shown him ended with the man at the centre burning a little more, and the Healer had never once counted him.
And he thought about something the Healer had said a few minutes before, almost proudly. I only had to let him notice in order.
A thing that needs a man to notice things in order needs him to be on time.
Rei decided to be late.
"Not tonight," he said.

He said it to the chair first, out loud, in the only voice it would listen to. He felt the question in the seam go unanswered and stay unanswered, like a phone left ringing in an empty flat. Then he said it again, more quietly, to the light. He said it the way someone would tell a man holding a heavy door that he could rest his arms for a moment. Rei stopped leaning on the balance point. He stopped asking it for anything.

The Axis felt the demand go out of the night. The bending in Rei's chest eased by a degree, then another. The light at the centre did not go out. It simply stopped breaking. For a heartbeat, before it sank back toward the wall, Rei thought the face looked at him with something like surprise.
He crossed the gravel to the rail and took his brother's hand.

It was Gin's hand. Cold, too still, and his. Under Rei's thumb the knuckles were faintly raised where small keys had been inked between them years ago. The Healer let him take it. Rei felt it decide to let him, the way a doctor lets a relative hold a patient's hand on the ward round.
"We're going home," Rei said. "Both of us. You can come too, since you're wearing him. But we're going."
For a long moment the Healer looked at him through Gin's eyes. Then it smiled. It was the dry half smile Gin always made and never followed with the joke.

"The ice is only soft tonight," it said. "Tomorrow is the last night. The sending fires. The dead go home and the wall goes thinner than this, and for longer. You have bought one day, Rei. I do not mind. A day is nothing to me." It glanced at the far bank. "It is nothing to that one either. Read your clocks."

Across the river Kaito turned and walked back down the far embankment into the dark, without hurry. Whatever looked out of him had seen enough. The chair would still be open tomorrow, and Kishin could wait one more night as easily as the Healer could.
Rei walked his brother off the embankment as the sky went grey over the yards.

They went back through the Kita-Ōji sidings. The old misery in the sheds had stopped leaning toward the river. It only lay there now, heavy and tired, like dust that had settled. A freight wagon stood on a siding with its doors open and nothing inside. Somewhere a dog barked twice and gave up.

They climbed toward Ōji. The dark hill of Asukayama rose beside them, and the crows in its trees had started their morning shouting. At the foot of the hill the tram tracks of the Toden line ran empty and shining. The first tram had not come yet. Under the elevated tracks at Ōji station the shutters were still down, and the only light came from a konbini, white and bright and humming. Through its window Rei could see a clerk mopping the floor in slow lines. A delivery van had stopped outside, and a man was unloading crates of morning newspapers in their plastic straps. He glanced up at the two brothers walking hand in hand, and then went back to his crates. Tokyo had seen stranger things at five in the morning.

They walked on through the shut streets toward home. The paper lanterns on the doorsteps were dark now, waiting for the last night. A grandmother in a cotton yukata was already sweeping the step in front of her house with a short broom, and she nodded to them as if she knew them. Maybe she did. They had lived in the ward all their lives. A newspaper boy on a bicycle passed them, standing on the pedals, his basket full.

Hand in hand, like boys. Neither of them spoke. Twice Gin's fingers pressed Rei's. Once, then once, then once. It was the knock from the inside. Their old signal. It was true, and not the Healer wearing truth like a coat.
At the foot of the stairs to the flat, in the first real light, the hand let go.
"I'll be at the rail tonight," the Healer said kindly, in Gin's voice. "So will you."

It turned and walked back the way they had come, in his brother's body and his brother's cardigan. Rei stood at the foot of the stairs and watched until the street bent and hid it. Somewhere behind the houses the first cicada of the day started up, then another.

Only when it was gone did he look down and see what it had left in his palm when it let go. It was a square of washi folded small and still warm from his brother's hand. On the outside, in Gin's upright pencil, there was a single letter. R.
